The head is thin and semi-transparent, usually fish skin or goatskin, with synthetic materials used recently. The frame has three or four rectangular slots where thin metal plates or ring-shaped jingles are fixed with hooks. The frame is about 45 to 50 cm across and about 5 to 7 cm deep. The wooden frame can be made by soaking the wood until soft, bending it around a heated metal cylinder and gluing the two ends; the head is then fixed with another wooden frame or with tacks. The fingers of the right hand first rest against their neighbours, then flick out suddenly, like a finger snap, to produce a fast, sharp, loud sound. A beginner can first practise dividing the work between the hands, then, once the drum is held steady, strike edge and centre separately, and only then add the flick of the fingers, controlling rhythm and volume.

The Behistun inscription of the sixth to fifth century BCE shows it is older than the rise of Islam and Sufism. In the Sassanid period (224–651) it was used at Nowruz, at court and in Iranian classical music, and it is connected with Mazdaean prayer and with the transmission of the radif and dastgah modes. It passed through the ancient Middle East, Greece and Rome into medieval Europe; the Arabs took it to Spain and the Ottomans carried it to Europe again in the seventeenth century. In the fifteenth century it is found only in Sufi ritual; it continued afterwards in Iranian traditional music, reached India with Persian influence, and in the twentieth century was used in South India and in Bollywood.

The dayereh (daf) is a frame drum from Iran, the Middle East and Central Asia, of the membranophone class, H-S number 211.311. Traditionally it has a circular wooden frame with rectangular slots holding small metal cymbals, and a head of fish skin or goatskin; metal frames and synthetic heads are also seen today. In playing, the left hand holds the drum and strikes the edge, the right hand strikes the centre, and the fingers hook onto their neighbours and then release suddenly, producing a loud, fast, sharp sound. It is used in Iranian traditional and classical music and at festivals such as Nowruz, and it also appears in Sufi ritual; in Pakistan it is a national instrument, and in India it appears in folk, protest and film music.
